passage:
Monday. Siddharth came home with a green badge from the school environment club. "I'm going to save the planet," he told his sister Simran.
Thursday. He brought back a book from a qawwali evening at a friend's house and played the same track for hours. "This is what matters," he said.
Sunday. He shaved his head with a friend from the photography club. Simran rolled her eyes. "Last week it was music."
"It's not a phase," he said. "I'm just trying stuff." He sat on the floor with his camera. "The tree-planting day is the one I keep going back to. When we finished, I felt like something was real. I don't know why."
Simran said nothing, but she took the seat beside him and looked at the photographs.

qa.q: What badge did Siddharth bring home on Monday?
qa.a: He brought a green badge from the school environment club.

qa.q: What does Siddharth's remark about the tree-planting day suggest about what he feels?
qa.a: It suggests that day left him feeling settled and sure that something was real, even though he cannot yet explain why.

qa.q: What could Simran do next to support Siddharth's search without dismissing it?
qa.a: Simran could ask what he liked about the tree-planting day and go along to one of the events, as she did with the photographs.

qa.q: How does Simran see Siddharth's changing enthusiasms from outside?
qa.a: Simran sees them as chaotic and rolls her eyes at the changes from week to week. She still sits beside him, so she takes his search seriously.

grounding: A teenager tries causes, music, photography and friend groups to find what feels worth living for; from outside it looks chaotic but is serious work.

passage:
Manoj, your mother says you've tried the band, the yoga club and the debate society in one year. Sit. I'll tell you about my sixteenth year. I'm Ujjwal, and I tried it all. I joined a rock band and quit after two months, spent a season in student politics, learned chess, and once stopped speaking to my friends for a week because I'd decided they were shallow.
My father said I was wasting my life. But my aunt said, "Let him look." I went from one thing to the next, and in the middle of all that mess, I began helping the small children at the mohalla library learn to read. I stayed. That one stuck, and I taught for forty years.
Nobody could see the search from outside. Inside, it was the hardest work I'd done.

qa.q: How long did Ujjwal teach, according to the story?
qa.a: Ujjwal taught for forty years.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling in the middle of the searching year?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt restless and unsure, going from one thing to the next, trying to find what felt worth doing.

qa.q: What turning point led Ujjwal to stay with one thing?
qa.a: Helping the small children at the mohalla library learn to read. Ujjwal stayed with it, and the search finally landed somewhere.

qa.q: How did the aunt see Ujjwal's search differently from the father?
qa.a: The aunt wanted the search allowed to run its course. The father saw it as wasted time.

grounding: A teenager experiments with bands, politics, chess and friends, searching for what is worth living for; it looks chaotic but is serious work.

passage: In Kumbakonam, Keerthana's family couldn't keep up with her. In June she joined the temple choir and practised at dawn. By August she'd quit and started a plastic-free club with three classmates, marching through the bazaar with cloth bags. In October she painted the backyard wall with a huge peacock and talked for a week about becoming an artist. "Next month it'll be something else," her brother Ujjwal said at dinner, rolling his eyes. Keerthana put down her spoon. "At least I'm looking." That night Ujjwal found her on the terrace with her notebook. On one page she had written: "Things that make me feel alive: singing with others, the club, painting the peacock." Under it: "Maybe it's making things with people." She looked up. "It's not random, anna. I'm trying to figure it out."

qa.q: What did Keerthana paint on the backyard wall?
qa.a: A huge peacock.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she said 'At least I'm looking'?
qa.a: She felt hurt and defensive at Ujjwal's teasing, because her search mattered deeply to her even if it looked random.

qa.q: How could Ujjwal support Keerthana's search?
qa.a: He could ask her what she liked about each thing, instead of predicting she'll quit, and maybe join her on the next one.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see Keerthana's changes at first?
qa.a: At first he sees them as random phases, rolling his eyes, until the notebook shows him she's taking it seriously.

grounding: Shows a teenager trying out faith, causes and art to find what feels worth living for, a search that looks chaotic outside but is serious inside.

passage: In Cape Town, Daniel's bedroom looked like three different people lived in it. There was a church youth group badge pinned to his curtain, a stack of vegan cookbooks from the library, and a borrowed bass guitar he was learning for a punk band. His mother called it "the Daniel museum." In one term he'd gone to Sunday services, then a climate march, then a poetry night. On Friday he told his friend Thabo, "I'm not trying to be cool. I just want to find the thing I'd get up at five in the morning for." Thabo laughed, then stopped when he saw Daniel's face. "Okay. So what's close?" Daniel thought. "The march. People who actually care." Thabo nodded. "Then maybe it's not the thing. Maybe it's the people."

qa.q: What did Daniel's mother call his bedroom?
qa.a: She called it 'the Daniel museum'.

qa.q: What does Daniel's face suggest when Thabo laughs?
qa.a: It suggests Daniel felt serious and a bit hurt, because this search matters deeply to him and isn't a joke.

qa.q: How did Thabo help once he stopped laughing?
qa.a: He asked what felt closest, which helped Daniel notice what he truly valued: people who actually care.

qa.q: How might Daniel's mother see his many interests?
qa.a: She seems to find them a bit chaotic and amusing, calling the room a museum, without seeing how serious the search is inside.

grounding: Shows a teenager trying different faiths, causes and scenes, seriously searching for what feels worth getting up for.

passage: At the community centre library in Mysuru, Sangeeta spread out four forms on the table: debate club, animal shelter volunteers, a Sanskrit reading circle, and a street theatre group. Ira, the librarian's daughter and her closest friend, sat opposite with a samosa. "Last month you were going to be a lawyer," Ira said. "I know." "The month before, a vet." "I know." Sangeeta stared at the forms. "I'm not bored, Ira. I'm scared I'll pick wrong and spend my life on something that doesn't matter." Ira stopped chewing. "So try two. One for your head, one for your heart." Sangeeta picked up the shelter form and the theatre form. Then she looked at the Sanskrit circle again, and slipped it into her bag too, just in case.

qa.q: How many forms did Sangeeta spread out on the table?
qa.a: Four forms.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta worried about?
qa.a: She was scared she would pick wrong and spend her life on something that doesn't matter.

qa.q: What small step did Ira suggest, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: Trying two things, one for the head and one for the heart, keeps the search going without Sangeeta having to decide everything at once.

qa.q: How does Ira see Sangeeta's changing plans at first?
qa.a: At first Ira teases her about wanting to be a lawyer and then a vet, until Sangeeta explains how serious it feels.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring causes, faith and art to find what feels worth living for, a search that is serious even if it looks chaotic.

passage:
Dear Mohit Bhaiya,
You asked on the phone why I sound "different every month". Fair question. In June I joined the lake clean-up group and wanted to be a marine biologist. In July I cut my hair short and wore only black. In August I went to the gurdwara with Harleen every morning just to sit in the quiet, even though our family isn't Sikh, and it felt more like home than almost anything. In September I left the quiz club because they only talk about ranks. Mummy calls it phases. Maybe. But each one told me something. The lake felt useful. The quiet felt true. The black clothes felt like a costume. I'm keeping two out of four, which honestly isn't bad.
Please don't laugh. I'm trying to find what's worth caring about, and I'm serious about it even if it looks messy.
Minakshi

qa.q: Where did Minakshi go every morning in August?
qa.a: Minakshi went to the gurdwara with Harleen, just to sit in the quiet.

qa.q: How does Minakshi feel about being called "different every month"?
qa.a: Minakshi feels a little defensive and worried about being laughed at, but also serious and hopeful about the search.

qa.q: How could Mohit reply in a way that helps?
qa.a: Mohit could skip the jokes and ask which of the two kept things feels most alive, taking the search as seriously as Minakshi does.

qa.q: How might Mummy's view of these changes differ from Minakshi's?
qa.a: Mummy sees phases that look random from outside, while for Minakshi each one is a careful test of what matters.

grounding: Shows a teenager trying out a cause, a faith space, a style and a group in a serious search for what feels worth caring about.
